title: Emoji Around the World
summary: Old emoticons, emoji, text faces, and stickers are still part of everyday messages. Their meanings can change with the country, online community, app, age group, and relationship.

cover.alt: Two adults at a rainy cafe table compare old text emoticons on one phone with modern colorful emoji on the other.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Old emoticons, emoji, text faces, and stickers are still part of everyday messages. Their meanings can change with the country, online community, app, age group, and relationship.

items.prompt: Which emoji do you use most often?
Have you ever misunderstood an emoji or sticker?
Do people of different ages use different faces in messages?

blocks.title: Part 1: Old Emoticons Are Still Alive
paragraphs: Before emoji became common, people made faces from keyboard symbols. These are called emoticons. A face such as :-) is read sideways, while XD shows strong laughter. They became popular in early email, forums, and chat rooms. They may look old now, but they have not disappeared. Emoticons that people still use in other countries include the Russian closing bracket, XD in gaming chats, and <3 in nostalgic messages.

Some habits developed in particular online communities. In Russian-language messages, a person may write one closing bracket, ), to show friendliness. Several brackets, ))), can suggest stronger warmth or laughter. In other countries, XD and <3 are still used in gaming communities or nostalgic posts. An old face can feel playful, sincere, or unfashionable, depending on who sends it.

images.alt: Three adults at a table and a friend on a laptop call still use old emoticons such as a smile, XD, and a heart on their phones.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: Old Emoticons Are Still Alive

items.prompt: Why can an old emoticon have different effects today?
items.answer: An old emoticon can seem friendly, playful, nostalgic, or unfashionable because different communities and age groups use it differently.
items.explanation: In your experience, which old emoticons or text faces would you still use?

blocks.title: Part 2: Emoji Meanings Can Travel and Change
paragraphs: Modern emoji grew from Japanese mobile communication. NTT DoCoMo released an influential set in 1999, and international Unicode support later helped emoji spread across devices and countries. However, the pictures travelled more easily than their original meanings.

For example, 🙏 can express thanks, a request, or an apology in Japan. Elsewhere, people may understand it mainly as prayer, and some users call it a high five. The face 😤 also shows change. Its steam originally suggested triumph or determination in a Japanese visual tradition, but many international users now read it as anger or frustration. Meaning therefore comes from both the picture’s source and the new setting where people use it.

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: Emoji Meanings Can Travel and Change

items.prompt: How did the meaning of 😤 change as it travelled?
items.answer: It originally suggested triumph or determination, but many users outside Japan now understand it as anger or frustration.

blocks.title: Part 3: Text Faces Look in Different Directions
paragraphs: A kaomoji is a text face that is usually read upright, not sideways. Examples include (^_^) for happiness, (T_T) for crying, and (¬_¬) for doubt or annoyance. These faces became strongly connected with Japanese online culture, although people now use them internationally.

Their design also shows an interesting contrast. In many Western emoticons, the mouth carries the main emotion: compare :-) with :-(. In kaomoji, the eyes often do more of the work. The rest of the face can add arms, tears, or movement. The international shrug is a small text picture made of bars, a round mouth, and raised arms. It carries a simple message: “I do not know” or “What can you do?”

images.alt: Two adults at a desk compare a notebook of sideways Western emoticons with a notebook of upright text faces.

blocks.title: Check: Part 3: Text Faces Look in Different Directions

items.prompt: What visual difference often separates kaomoji from older Western emoticons?
items.answer: Kaomoji are usually upright and often emphasize the eyes, while older Western emoticons are commonly sideways and emphasize the mouth.

blocks.title: Part 4: Stickers Create Local Chat Habits
paragraphs: Stickers are larger and more detailed than ordinary emoji. They may show a full character, include words, or move through animation. Because apps sell or provide different sticker collections, local messaging habits can develop around particular characters.

LINE stickers are especially familiar in Japan, Thailand, and Taiwan. LINE characters such as Brown and Cony began as messaging stickers and later appeared on many physical products. In South Korea, KakaoTalk has its own popular character stickers, while WeChat users in China often exchange animated images and user-made sticker collections. A sticker can soften a refusal, show thanks, or end a conversation warmly. However, someone outside that app community may not recognize the character or understand the social tone.

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: Stickers Create Local Chat Habits

items.prompt: Why are sticker meanings often connected to particular places or communities?
items.answer: Sticker meanings are connected to places and communities because different apps, characters, collections, and social habits are popular in different regions.

blocks.title: Part 5: Read the Person, Platform, and Situation
paragraphs: There is no perfect international emoji dictionary. A useful method is to consider three things: the person, the platform, and the situation. First, age and relationship matter. A simple 🙂 may seem pleasantly polite to one person but cold or passive-aggressive to another. Second, platforms sometimes display the same emoji with slightly different designs. A small change in the eyes or mouth can change its emotional effect.

Finally, online communities create new meanings. In many English-language social media spaces, 💀 can mean “That was so funny I died,” rather than actual danger or death. Old faces can also return as jokes or signs of nostalgia. When meaning is unclear, the surrounding message and the sender’s usual style are often more useful than the symbol alone.

images.alt: Three adults in an office, a kitchen, and a train read similar emoji in different situations, with different reactions.

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: Read the Person, Platform, and Situation

items.prompt: What three kinds of context can help you understand an unfamiliar emoji?
items.answer: You can consider who sent it, how the platform displays it, and what is happening in the conversation.
